schools.summary: Gill accepts the month-after reading on the authority of the versions and Josephus, places Jabesh in Manasseh beyond Jordan, and holds that the messengers came to Gibeah knowing the chosen king lived there.

Henry lays the capitulation to apostasy, itemises the three objects of the mutilation, reads the seven days' respite as Nahash's bravado overruled by providence, and says the people would sooner shed tears for their brethren than blood.

Clarke rejects the month-after addition as of little authority, quotes Theodoret on the shield and the right eye, and argues the message was addressed to the people and not to Saul; Wesley leaves the date open and notices that one eye is left for base service.

Ellicott makes the invasion revenge for Jephthah's defeat, tells the old tie between Jabesh and Benjamin in full, and has the respite asked in hope of Saul himself; Keil and Delitzsch reject the emendation behind the Greek and settle who does the thrusting out.

sides.position: A month after Saul was chosen, with the Greek and Latin versions and Josephus
The addition is of very little authority and should be set aside
Before the election, as a later chapter shows; the emendation behind the Greek is unsupported by every other version
Open between the two, the invasion or only its preparation having prompted the demand for a king

debates.question: Why did Jabesh offer to capitulate?

sides.position: They were in no condition to risk a war
Isolation and distance from the centre of the nation
They saw no likelihood of relief from their brethren
Apostasy: having lost the virtue of Israelites they lost the valour of them

debates.question: Did the besieged know Israel had a king?

sides.position: No: the embassy was to all Israel and the message was addressed to the people, not to Saul
Yes: they sent to Gibeah directly, and asked the respite in hope of Saul

outliers.note: Alone in weighing what the condition leaves as well as what it takes, that one eye remains so the men may still serve in any mean and base office.

themes: Nahash the Ammonite encamped against Jabeshgilead
that I may thrust out all your right eyes
give us seven days' respite
all the people lifted up their voices, and wept
1.pericope_label: Nahash the Ammonite: on this condition, that I thrust out all your right eyes

schools.summary: Gill explains the king still at the herd by his want of inauguration, state and revenue, and reads the Spirit as pity, wisdom and fortitude together, citing the Targum.
Henry makes the ploughing humility, itemises the anger, finds the threat against the oxen mild by comparison with an earlier summons, and calls the joining of Samuel's name modesty.

Clarke dismantles the moral drawn from kings taken from the plough, reduces the kindled anger to excited courage, and compares the Highland bloody cross; Wesley gives the reason behind the method and takes the fear as sent by God.

Ellicott makes the ploughing policy while the kingship was kept in the background, has the Spirit endue him as it had the judges, and quotes Ewald on the Norwegian war-arrow; Keil and Delitzsch refer the anger to the shame meant for Israel and refuse the panic-terror reading.

debates.question: Why was the elected king still following the herd?

sides.position: Necessity: not yet inaugurated, with no state, revenue or business while Samuel still acted
Policy: the kingship was kept in the background until something should bring it forward
Humility: he did not think it beneath him to know the state of his own flocks
A providential interval, while he waited for a call

debates.question: What does the kindled anger amount to?

sides.position: No more than courage greatly excited and confidence of success
Anger at the shame the Ammonites meant to fix on all Israel
Anger at four things: the Ammonites, the men of Jabesh, their delay, and the weeping

debates.question: Why does Samuel's name stand beside Saul's in the summons?

sides.position: Saul as king still recognised the authority Samuel held as prophet
Samuel was present, and his name added weight
Modesty: Saul would not execute the king's office without regard to the prophet's

outliers.note: Alone in dismantling the moral the others draw from a king at the plough, since in ancient times agriculture was the only employment and every dignity had to be filled from that class.

themes: Saul came after the herd out of the field
the Spirit of God came upon Saul
he took a yoke of oxen, and hewed them in pieces
the fear of the Lord fell on the people
5.pericope_label: The Spirit of God came upon Saul: he hewed the oxen in pieces

schools.summary: Gill records the reading that makes Bezek not a place but a counting-token, a stone or a fragment or a branch brought by each man.

Clarke doubts the whole tradition of the numbers and suspects the Hebrew itself of exaggeration, times the night march across Jordan, and reads the completeness of the rout from the closing detail; Wesley makes the separate numbering of Judah a credit to that tribe.

Ellicott locates Bezek in the plain of Jezreel, allows copyists' errors in numbers while rejecting the charge that the verse is a reviser's insertion, and fixes the hours of the morning watch; Keil and Delitzsch defend the figures as a general levy and read the separate mention of Judah as an early trace of secession.

debates.question: Are the numbers at Bezek to be trusted?

sides.position: Yes: this was a general levy of the whole people, not a regular army
No: the versions disagree wildly and even the Hebrew looks exaggerated by some ancient scribe
The verse is authentic, though numbers in these books suffer from copyists
An early trace of the separation that ended in secession, the southern tribe standing apart until it had a king of its own
To Judah's honour: the tribe promised the kingdom submitted readily to a king of another tribe

outliers.note: Alone in preserving the reading that takes the word for Bezek as a common noun, so that the king's servants counted not men but stones, potsherds or branches brought by each.

themes: he numbered them in Bezek
three hundred thousand, and the men of Judah thirty thousand
to morrow, by that time the sun be hot
they came into the midst of the host in the morning watch
8.pericope_label: They came out as one man: Israel three hundred thousand, Judah thirty thousand

schools.summary: Gill reasons out how a man of Samuel's years kept up with the march, and alone glances forward to the fact that Saul's clemency did not last.
Henry explains why the motion went to Samuel rather than to Saul, observes that victory did more to confirm the title than either lot or anointing, and gives two reasons for the pardon.
Clarke sets the king's answer against the soldiers' proposal and generalises about what victory does to a common soldier.

Ellicott measures the seer's standing by the people turning to him in the first flush of the victory and calls the pardon wise as well as generous; Keil and Delitzsch settle the form of the question and find magnanimity and genuine piety in the answer.

debates.question: What kind of act was Saul's refusal to execute his opponents?

sides.position: Magnanimity and genuine piety together
Generous and politically wise, since vengeance would have begun lasting feuds
Lenity and policy at the opening of a reign, and a temper that did not continue with him
Fitting to a day of triumph, and better than killing, since an enemy reclaimed is the greater gain

outliers.note: Alone in generalising from the demand to the character of soldiers, that the common soldier is scarcely ever inspired by a victory to magnanimity: having shed blood he wishes to shed more.

themes: who is he that said, Shall Saul reign over us?
bring the men, that we may put them to death
there shall not a man be put to death this day
to day the Lord hath wrought salvation in Israel
12.pericope_label: Who is he that said, Shall Saul reign over us? There shall not a man be put to death

schools.summary: Gill has Samuel fall in with the pardon and propose Gilgal partly to turn the people off their demand and partly to take them in a good temper.

Clarke holds a second anointing likely and reports that Josephus says so plainly, appends a correspondent's letter comparing the hewn oxen with the Highland fiery cross, and ends on the kingdom soon lost through imprudence; Wesley reads the timing as Samuel's prudence and fidelity.

Ellicott refuses a fresh anointing against the Greek version, takes the convention for a national confirmation of the election at Mizpeh, reads the phrase before the Lord of the ark or the high priest, and marks the generosity of a seer presenting the man who superseded him.

debates.question: Was Saul anointed a second time at Gilgal?

sides.position: Likely, the first unction having been private and the appointment not generally known; Josephus says so
No: the Greek version's reading is not to be followed, the convention being a solemn confirmation only

debates.question: Why was the assembly called at this moment?

sides.position: To divert the people from their demand for the offenders' lives while their temper was good
Because the confirmation had been suspended while they were disaffected, and their hearts were now set on him
Because the election at Mizpeh had met with murmurings that wanted repairing

outliers.note: Alone in appending to the chapter's last verse a long letter from a correspondent on the hewn oxen, comparing the Highland fiery cross and the Scandinavian penalty of death and burning with Israel's milder forfeiture of the beasts.

themes: come, and let us go to Gilgal, and renew the kingdom there

Saul and all the men of Israel rejoiced greatly
14.pericope_label: Come, let us go to Gilgal and renew the kingdom there
